strengths: Addresses a genuinely under-explored and timely problem: extending MLLMs from single-image to multi-frame spatial understanding (depth, correspondence, dynamic perception).

Substantial data effort: a 27M-sample MultiSPA dataset and a multi-task benchmark with diverse input referencing (dots, coordinates, semantic labels) and output formats (qualitative, scalar, MCQ, vector, coordinate), with a documented generation pipeline and released code listings (Listings 1-4).

External validation on the BLINK benchmark (Table 3) is a real strength: Multi-SpatialMLLM reaches 84.3 average, outperforming GPT-4o (73.8) and other baselines, suggesting transferable multi-frame spatial ability rather than only fitting the authors' own distribution.
Shows multi-task synergy (Table 5) and rough parity on standard VQA benchmarks (Table 4), supporting that the fine-tuning does not simply degrade general capability.
The appendix provides useful implementation detail (image-pair sampling, BFS minimum-coverage search, rigid-body segmentation, rotation-angle definitions), which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: The headline results (Table 2) are computed on the authors' own MultiSPA benchmark, which is generated by the same pipeline that produces the training data. Although the benchmark uses held-out scenes, the questions, templates, and answer formats share the training distribution, so the very large margins over zero-shot proprietary models (~56 vs ~28) conflate genuine spatial reasoning with familiarity with the task/format conventions. This is a material validity concern, not merely presentation.

Several core tasks are scale-ambiguous from RGB images alone and therefore arguably ill-posed: absolute depth in mm, object size (height/width/length) in mm, and camera/object displacement vectors in mm. A model seeing only images cannot in principle recover absolute metric scale without strong scene priors. The high reported accuracies on these tasks (e.g., Depth Value 75.33%, Object Size 49.11%) therefore likely reflect exploitation of dataset-level priors/bias rather than the spatial understanding the paper claims to measure, undermining the central thesis.

The 'emergence of spatial understanding' claim rests on a single small experiment (Table 6) in which only the 26B variant improves, but that variant also uses a different 6B vision encoder and 20B LLM, so model scale is confounded with encoder/LLM configuration. The evidence is too thin for an 'emergent' claim, and the 'Baseline v.s. Hard' column is ambiguously presented.

Only one base model (InternVL2-8B) is fine-tuned, and the three advertised capabilities (depth perception, visual correspondence, dynamic perception) are never ablated, so it is unclear which components drive the gains or whether they are all necessary.

The proprietary-model comparison is not apples-to-apples: Multi-SpatialMLLM is fine-tuned on 3M task-specific samples while proprietary models are zero-shot, and the authors additionally apply extra prompts and GPT-4o post-processing to force baselines into the required answer format. This handling can bias comparisons in the authors' favor.

Despite the 'multi-frame' framing, the depth-perception subtasks are single-image, and the paper itself acknowledges experiments only use two-view scenarios; the claimed multi-frame capability is narrower than advertised.
No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported, and the 20%/5% tolerance-based accuracy metrics are lenient, making the magnitude of the reported gains hard to interpret.

Key resources (dataset, benchmark, project page) appear to be placeholders ('Correspondence/Project Page' blank), so actual availability and reproducibility of the 27M-sample dataset cannot be verified from the manuscript.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely under-explored problem: multi-frame (vs. single-image) spatial understanding in MLLMs, with a well-motivated framing around depth, correspondence, and dynamic perception (Structure-from-Motion inspired).

Substantial data contribution: the MultiSPA dataset (27M+ QA pairs from 1.1M images across ScanNet, PStudio, ADT, TAPVid3D) and an accompanying benchmark with 26 subtasks is a valuable community resource, with the pipeline carefully engineered (overlap-ratio binning, BFS minimum-coverage-set search, clustering-based rigid-body segmentation).

Strong and clear empirical gains: Multi-SpatialMLLM (8B) achieves ~36% average improvement over the base model and matches/outperforms much larger proprietary models (GPT-4o, Claude-3.5, Gemini-2.0) on the MultiSPA benchmark, with near-zero baselines on hard quantitative subtasks.

Evidence for scalability (Fig. 4) and multi-task synergy (Tab. 5) is provided, plus zero-shot generalization to BLINK and preservation of general VQA/OCR/reasoning performance (Tab. 4), which supports the claim that the model is a general-purpose MLLM rather than overfit.

Reproducibility is comparatively strong: appendix includes data templates, sampling algorithms, and segmentation/coverage code snippets, and details of source datasets and training hyperparameters are given.
Practical downstream demonstration (robotics reward annotation, Fig. 5) adds usefulness beyond benchmark numbers.
weaknesses: The 'multi-frame' claim is only partially realized: experiments and benchmark are restricted to two-view (image-pair) settings, so the method does not actually demonstrate reasoning over more than two frames despite the title and framing (acknowledged in Appendix H).
Benchmark is thin per subtask: only 300 held-out samples per subtask (7,800 total), which limits statistical reliability of the per-subtask comparisons and of the 'emergence' analysis.

Evaluation breadth is limited: the model is only built on InternVL2 (8B) with LoRA rank 16; no other base MLLM family is fine-tuned, so the generality of the data's benefit across architectures is not established.

No direct comparison with concurrent multi-frame spatial work (e.g., SAT [54]) is performed, and no comparison with other spatial-tuning methods (SpatialVLM/SpatialRGPT) on a common setting, weakening the positioning claim.
The 'emergent spatial understanding' claim is preliminary and based on a single multiple-choice task and a single 26B variant; the causal explanation (model capacity) is speculative.

Some evaluation criteria are somewhat arbitrary (20% relative error for scalars/vectors, 5% image-width for pixel coordinates) and no sensitivity analysis or human/upper-bound baseline is provided to calibrate task difficulty.

Absolute accuracies on several quantitative tasks (camera translation vector 18%, object movement vector 12.9%, camera degree 45.5%) are low, raising the question of whether the model truly solves these tasks or whether they mainly reflect partial progress; more analysis of failure modes would strengthen the claims.

Potential train/benchmark source overlap: both draw from ScanNet/TAPVid3D; the paper asserts benchmark images come from 'distinct scenes or scenarios' but provides no explicit overlap-verification evidence.
Training uses only a 3M subset of the 27M samples (one epoch), so the reported benefits may not reflect the full dataset; this is understandable given compute but is not fully analyzed.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: equipping MLLMs with multi-frame spatial understanding (depth, visual correspondence, camera/object motion), which is important for robotics and embodied applications beyond single-image spatial QA.

Introduces a large-scale dataset (MultiSPA, 27M QA samples from 1.1M images) built via a principled data engine that back-projects point clouds and establishes pixel correspondences on top of annotated 3D/4D datasets (ScanNet, PStudio, ADT, TAPVid3D), rather than relying on noisy off-the-shelf depth/segmentation models.

Provides a comprehensive benchmark spanning diverse task types and output formats (qualitative, scalar, MCQ, coordinate, vector), which is broader than prior single-image or MCQ-limited spatial benchmarks.

Strong and consistent empirical results: an 8B model with LoRA surpasses far larger proprietary systems (GPT-4o, Claude-3.5, Gemini-2.0) on the MultiSPA benchmark, with a reported ~36% average gain over the InternVL2 base model.

Demonstrates generalization: zero-shot transfer to BLINK (outperforming proprietary models on several splits) while retaining parity on standard VQA benchmarks, suggesting the model is not overfit to multi-frame spatial reasoning.

Includes scalability analysis (consistent gains with data volume and model size, Fig. 4), evidence of multi-task synergy (Table 5), and a preliminary emergence study (Table 6) that collectively strengthen the empirical story.
Practical downstream demonstration as a multi-frame reward annotator for robotics (Fig. 5), illustrating concrete usefulness.

Good reproducibility signals: data-format specification, prompt templates, rotation-angle derivation, and code listings for image-pair sampling, coverage-set search, and rigid-body segmentation are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Ground-truth quality is not adequately validated. QA answers are generated from back-projected point clouds and GPT-4o templates, so depth, correspondence, and motion targets inherit noise from the source reconstructions and are never checked against human annotation; a quality-control / human-verification study is missing.

Evaluation thresholds are permissive and could inflate reported accuracy: scalar/vector answers are marked correct within 20% of the ground-truth norm, and pixel coordinates within 5% of image width. The sensitivity of headline numbers to these thresholds is not analyzed.

The 'multi-frame' framing is largely limited to image pairs in practice (acknowledged in the Limitations), which weakens the central claim and leaves the ambiguity between object motion and camera motion in a single pair (explicitly noted in the prompts) only partially resolved.

Baseline coverage is narrow: comparisons focus on InternVL2 variants and proprietary APIs, with no head-to-head comparison to the most closely related multi-frame work (e.g., SAT) on the proposed benchmark, and no ablation across alternative base MLLMs to establish generality of the training recipe.
The benchmark is small per subtask (300 held-out samples each) and no statistical significance or confidence intervals are reported, so small differences among models are difficult to interpret.

The emergence claim rests on a single multiple-choice correspondence task with one Hard/Easy manipulation; the authors themselves label it preliminary, so the interpretation of 'emergence' remains speculative.
Scene/domain diversity is bounded by the source datasets (indoor scans and egocentric recordings); generalization to outdoor/driving or larger-scale scenes is not demonstrated.
Object-size perception accuracy remains relatively low (~49%) and depends on semantic-label referencing, but the practical implications and error modes are not analyzed.

strengths: Introduces MultiSPA, a large-scale multi-frame spatial understanding dataset and benchmark with 27M+ QA samples spanning depth perception, visual correspondence, camera movement, object movement, and object size, covering diverse input reference modes and output formats.

Provides a detailed and technically grounded data generation pipeline that leverages annotated 3D/4D datasets, point-cloud backprojection, balanced overlap sampling, BFS-based coverage search, and rigid-body clustering, with code snippets and templates in the appendix.

Experimental results are extensive: the fine-tuned 8B Multi-SpatialMLLM substantially outperforms zero-shot baselines and proprietary models on the proposed benchmark, generalizes to held-out BLINK and 3D benchmarks, preserves general VQA performance, and shows positive scaling trends and multi-task synergy.

The paper offers useful practical insights, including the importance of tuning the vision encoder, the benefit of task diversity beyond data volume, and a qualitative demonstration of multi-frame reward annotation for robotics.
weaknesses: The main model is trained on only a 3M subset of the 27M-sample dataset, so the paper does not fully demonstrate the value of the complete MultiSPA dataset; the scalability analysis is limited to a subset and mainly one camera-vector task.

The proposed benchmark is generated from the same pipeline and source datasets as training, and with a relatively small evaluation set (7,800 QA samples); independent validation relies mainly on BLINK and a few external benchmarks, which may not fully establish broad multi-frame spatial reasoning.
Comparisons with proprietary models use prompt engineering and GPT-4 post-processing, and there are no error bars or repeated runs, making the baseline comparison less rigorous.

Some claims are preliminary or overstated: the emergent spatial capability evidence is limited to a single setting without repeated seeds, the robotics reward-annotation demo is qualitative and potentially cherry-picked, and the paper reports matching expert models while Table 9 shows lower depth accuracy than Depth-Anything.

A few technical/presentational issues remain, such as the relative camera pose translation notation written as E_j[0:3,3] instead of E_i^j[0:3,3], the loose 20% relative L2 tolerance for scalar/vector evaluation, and the '36% gain' phrasing versus the reported +35.68 percentage points.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely gap: extending MLLM spatial reasoning beyond single images toward multi-frame/embodied settings, which is relevant for robotics and autonomous systems.

Constructs a large-scale dataset (27M+ samples) via a principled pipeline that leverages existing 3D annotations (point clouds, camera extrinsics/intrinsics, depth maps, 3D tracking) rather than noisy off-the-shelf perception modules, and uses balanced bin-based sampling to mitigate the long-tailed overlap/motion distributions (Sec. 3.2, Listings 1-3).

The benchmark is more diverse than prior MCQ-only spatial benchmarks, supporting multiple referencing modalities (dots, pixel coordinates, semantic labels) and multiple output formats (qualitative, scalar, MCQ, vector, coordinate), with task-specific evaluation criteria (Sec. 3.3).

Provides a fair, same-backbone external generalization result on BLINK (Sec. 4.2, Tab. 3), where the fine-tuned model improves ~26.4% over the base InternVL, which is stronger evidence than the in-distribution benchmark.
Includes useful auxiliary analyses such as multi-task synergy (Tabs. 5, 12, 13), a forgetting curve on general VQA (Fig. 6), and data/model scaling trends (Fig. 4).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the approach is essentially LoRA fine-tuning of InternVL2 on a curated dataset, conceptually close to SpatialVLM/SpatialRGPT, extended to two-frame inputs. The 'multi-frame' framing is overstated, since the data is predominantly two-frame pairs (Appendix L/M confirm this; multi-frame is only probed by inserting intermediate frames in Tab. 14).

Overclaimed headline results: the '36% average gain' and the claim of 'surpassing even larger proprietary models' (Tab. 2) compare a model fine-tuned on the exact task distribution against zero-shot GPT-4o/Claude-3.5/Gemini-2.0 that were merely prompted to 'guess.' This asymmetry materially inflates the apparent contribution and should not be presented as a like-for-like comparison.

The primary MultiSPA benchmark is in-distribution: it is generated from the same source datasets (ScanNet, TAPVid3D) and the same templates as training, held out only by scene. High scores therefore largely reflect fitting the task templates rather than demonstrating generalizable spatial reasoning.

Several quantitative tasks are ill-posed and likely measure dataset fit rather than spatial understanding. Predicting depth, camera translation distance, and object size in millimetres from monocular images is not well-defined without metric scale; the reported accuracies (e.g., depth value 75.33, camera translation distance 42.33) plausibly exploit scene-specific scale priors, and the 20% relative-error tolerance for scalars/vectors is loose.

The 'emergence' claim (Sec. 4.3, abstract) rests on a single multiple-choice visual-correspondence experiment (Tab. 6); the authors themselves state that 'further investigation is required,' so the abstract's 'emergent spatial capabilities' is not adequately supported.

Evaluation robustness is thin: no variance/error bars or multiple seeds are reported for the benchmark, and the 8B model is trained on only 3M of the 27M samples, so the dataset-scale claims are not fully validated by the presented results.

strengths: Introduces MultiSPA, a large-scale multi-frame spatial understanding dataset with 27M+ QA samples over 1.1M images, covering five core tasks (depth, visual correspondence, camera movement, object movement, object size) with diverse input referencing and output formats.

Proposes a scalable data generation pipeline built on existing annotated 3D/4D datasets (ScanNet, ADT, PStudio, TAPVid3D) that computes visible points, overlap ratios, camera poses, and object trajectories to construct multi-frame spatial QA pairs.

Provides a unified MultiSPA benchmark with 26 subtasks and consistent evaluation metrics, revealing that current MLLMs struggle severely on quantitative spatial tasks such as coordinate correspondence, depth values, and camera/object movement vectors.

Shows strong empirical gains: Multi-SpatialMLLM, an 8B LoRA-tuned model, achieves 56.11 average accuracy versus 20-31 for baselines and proprietary models on MultiSPA, and also generalizes to BLINK (84.3 average vs. 73.8 for GPT-4o).

Demonstrates generalization and multi-task synergy: improvements transfer to held-out spatial benchmarks, standard VQA performance is largely preserved, and adding data from related tasks consistently improves challenging vector prediction tasks.

Includes useful scaling analysis (data/model size) and practical demonstrations such as zero-shot robot arm scenarios and use as a multi-frame reward annotator, suggesting downstream value beyond benchmark performance.
The paper is well organized, with extensive supplementary details, templates, and code listings that aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The dataset and benchmark are generated automatically using existing annotations and GPT-4o templates, but lack human verification of QA quality, ambiguity, and potential label noise, especially for small camera motions and occluded points in dynamic scenes.

Evaluation thresholds are somewhat loose (e.g., 5% image-width tolerance for coordinates, 20% relative error for scalars/vectors), which may inflate reported accuracies and hide the severity of quantitative errors.
Multi-frame reasoning is mostly limited to image pairs; generalization to more than two frames is only tested on camera direction prediction, not on the other spatial tasks.

The 'emergent' spatial ability claim is based on a single multiple-choice visual correspondence study; only the 26B variant improves over its baseline, making the interpretation speculative and overclaimed.
Comparisons with proprietary models depend on GPT-4 post-processing and prompting to enforce output formats, which may not fully reflect those models' true spatial reasoning capabilities.

The main model is trained on only a 3M subset of the 27M+ MultiSPA samples, so the full dataset's potential is not fully exploited, and the paper does not explore whether larger-scale training closes remaining gaps.
The robot reward-annotation demonstration is qualitative and trend-based rather than a quantitative evaluation, so the claimed robotics utility remains preliminary.
Object size perception uses only two images due to computational constraints, which may not always cover an object's full 3D dimensions despite the proposed BFS minimum-coverage-set search.
